grammar.title: Phone openers with Alo and Ko je tamo?
grammar.explanation: Start a call with Alo? Then ask Ko je tamo? When you need a name. Keep both lines short and clear. Present-tense phone talk is enough, even for an urgent cat emergency.

grammar.title: Šta, kada, and zašto
grammar.explanation: Use šta for what, kada for when, and zašto for why. Pair each question word with a present verb you already know. These three help you gather facts fast on a call.

grammar.title: Urgent present lines
grammar.explanation: Hitno je! Flags urgency. Nestala describes a feminine missing subject, such as Mrvica. Add Molim vas when you ask a stranger for help, by phone or on the street.

culture.title: Calls beside the tram
culture.body: Sarajevo trams slide past cafés where people still step outside to take a call in clearer air. Ana phones Emir when Mrvica disappears near the tracks, and suddenly every question word matters. Ko, šta, kada, and zašto turn her panic into a checklist she can repeat under stress. Mobile connection is ordinary now, yet the voice on the line still carries real care across a noisy street. A simple Alo? Can open both small talk and a true emergency, before anyone even explains the problem. Phone phrases like these belong on a noisy street, not just in a quiet classroom.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Phone questions that gather facts
lessonBlocks.body: Start with the phone words: telefon, poziv, alo, broj, and veza, before the emergency story begins. Practice Alo? And Ko je tamo? Until both openers sound natural on the first try. Then drill šta, kada, and zašto with short present-tense answers so the facts come out in order. Ana calls from near a tram stop while Emir asks for details without wasting time. Keep the lines sharp. A missing cat won't wait for a grammar lesson. Try asking all four question words out loud, then answer each one in one calm present-tense sentence. Keep that checklist order steady even under pressure.
tips: Start with Alo? Before you ask anything else.
Use one question word at a time.
Answer with a short present-tense sentence.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. The Mrvica emergency call
lessonBlocks.body: Build the emergency call as a sequence you can run even when you feel rushed. Say Hitno je! Then Mrvica je nestala! Then ask for help with molim vas in a clear voice. Use Čujem te dobro when the connection is good and you want to slow the other person down. Amira joins the search on another line, and the tram keeps moving beside the café windows. Close the call with a plan, still in the present: Idemo sad. Practice until the question words feel like a calm checklist instead of a scramble of panic. Try running through the full call once without looking at your notes.
tips: Say Hitno je! Early if the problem is urgent.
Add molim vas when you ask for help.
Confirm the connection with Čujem te dobro.

funFacts.title: Alo is the phone hello
funFacts.body: Bosnian phone calls often open with Alo? Rather than a street greeting. The short sound checks the line and invites the other person to speak. Keep it separate from Zdravo. The medium changes the first word.

funFacts.title: Trams frame everyday calls
funFacts.body: Sarajevo trams run through central corridors where people move between errands and cafés. Taking a call beside the tracks is a normal city scene. The tram keeps this emergency story local and on the move. Background noise on the line becomes part of the listening practice.

funFacts.title: Question words form a checklist
funFacts.body: Ko, šta, kada, and zašto help a panicked speaker slow down. Each word asks for one kind of fact. Used together, they organize an urgent conversation. Book 1 teaches them as present-tense tools you can use right away, not as abstract grammar labels.

funFacts.title: Mrvica keeps the stakes personal
funFacts.body: A missing cat is a comic emergency with real feeling behind it. The cast cares, so you care enough to repeat the lines. That personal stake is what makes phone phrases stick. Humor and urgency can share the same call.

civicContext.title: An opaque U.S.-linked gas deal bypassed normal tender rules
civicContext.body: An urgent phone call home still travels through a country that depends on outside energy patrons. Bosnia and Herzegovina imports nearly all of its natural gas along a Russian-linked route through neighboring systems. In 2026 the Federation moved to name a U.S. Company linked to Trump-aligned investors as developer of the Southern Interconnection, without a normal open tender. European Union officials warned that the special law could threaten transparency standards and aid. The pipeline fight shows how big contracts can be decided by political pressure rather than a fair, open contest.
